newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military sex cases worry Pentagon.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military sex cases worry Pentagon.

text.p: The conviction of an Army drill sergeant on multiple rape charges has deepened the Pentagon's worry that the U.S. military is still seen as an abusive male bastion that scoffs at equality for women.

Tuesday's decision by an Army jury at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, that Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson raped six female recruits came in the most prominent case of a major sexual scandal involving the power and discretion of male trainers.

Military officials and private analysts say the scandal at Aberdeen and other bases adds insult to a growing number of military sex harassment and abuse cases in recent years, sparking problems far beyond base gates and U.S. borders.

"It does damage to the military at home and abroad. And even more seriously than public perception, it diverts the energies of military and defence leaders," former Defence Undersecretary Fred Ikle told Reuters.

"The prominence and frequency of these cases is troubling, It hurts the military's self-esteem," added Ikle, who served in the Reagan administration and is now an analyst at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington think tank.

From Defence Secretary William Cohen down through the ranks, the military worries about high-profile incidents carried on television and in newspapers since the Navy's 1991 "Tailhook" sexual abuse scandal in which male fliers fondled and abused women at a Las Vegas Hotel.

The September 1995 rape of a Japanese schoolgirl by three American servicemen on Okinawa badly bruised U.S.-Japan relations and prompted the Pentagon to bow to demands by residents on the Japanese island to sharply lower the profile of America's military presence there.
Showing concern over other incidents involving U.S. troops in Japan since that time, Cohen repeatedly reminded troops during a recent visit to Japan that they were "ambassadors" of the United States.

"You can do 100 good deeds and you will get credit for it," he said. "On the other hand, one bad deed, and that makes the headline news and changes people's perception of what we are doing as a nation."

To be e fair, the U.S. military is pushing strict rules against sexual misconduct, including jail terms for adultery, and is embarked on an active effort to train the services to respect the rights of women in the armed forces.

"I think that (Aberdeen) jury came to a decision based on the evidence and not just to send a message," said one senior defence official, who did not want to be identified. "Having said that, a message certainly nees to be sent."

He and others at the sprawling headquarters of the U.S. military fear that recruiting of women will drop because of abuse of young females by male Army trainers at Aberdeen; Fort Leonard Wood, Mo., Fort Bliss, Texas, and other bases.
Officials at Fort Bliss announced on April 25 that three officers had been kicked out of the military and sent to prison for sexual misconduct with female enlisted soldiers.
Under military rules, officers are not even allowed to mix socially with enlisted personnel much less have consentual or other sex with subordinates.

There are now about 192,000 women in the 1.4 million-member U.S. military. That is about 13 per cent and the Pentagon worries that the percentage could erode despite pressure on men and formal training programmes to treat female comrades equally.
"It's easy for us to keep saying that the military is very tough on this kind of kind of thing, that we don't tolerate prejudice and we are training people right," an Army general told Reuters.

"But the evidence flies in the face of that. People around the world read the stories when our men attack young recruits, degrade women in Las Vegas and rape a little girl," added the officer, who asked not to be identified.
Many analysts predicted that things would get dramatically better after Tailhook, but the cases keep popping up despite punishment of those who violate the law.

Simpson, 32, could face life in prison when he is sentenced next week for his conviction on 18 counts of rape. He already pleaded guilty to 11 counts of consensual sex and five counts of propositioning, for which he faced a maximum sentence of 32 years in prison.
Cohen declined to comment directly on the case on Wednesday because Simpson still has a right to appeal.
"The department is looking intensively into the issue," he told reporters. "We believe that the problem has to be dealt with head-on."
Cohen said the armed forces had largely overcome the problems of racism and druge abuse in the ranks "and I'm sure we will do the same with respect to this issue."
